transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-07
Time: 15:00 EST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Devon Park (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (NovaHealth Infra), Maya Chen (NovaHealth SRE), Irene Gomez (NovaHealth Security), Sam Torres (Product)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 45 minutes, agenda is quick recap of last week's pilot numbers, then focused on dedicated sizing and autoscaling / burst planning. Devon's gonna lead the sizing part.
[00:12] Raj Patel: Thanks Lena, yeah we saw the initial throughput numbers, a couple clarifications before we get in - our peak window is 8:30-10:30 PST and around 14:00 PST has a smaller spike. We'll share exact histograms.
[00:25] Devon Park: Great, thanks Raj. Quick note - the dedicated pool we spun up in the pilot was 4x A100 equivalents, with the Redwood runtime set to default batch settings. We instrumented per-route latency and token cost.
[00:37] Maya Chen: When you say A100 equivalents, are those v3 or v4? We run some inference on v4 in prod and perf differs.
[00:44] Devon Park: Good call, sorry shorthand - these are v4-like instances; the runtime was measuring on Ampere-NV4 cluster, so latency numbers will be slightly better than older v3 setups.
[00:56] Sam Torres: For context, our SLO for user-facing assistant is 200 ms p50 and 600 ms p95 for responses under 256 tokens.
[01:06] Devon Park: Noted. In the pilot today, our observed p50 was ~160 ms and p95 ~520 ms for the 128 token median routes; longer routes hit ~800 ms p95. There's some room for kernel selection and quantization wins.
[01:20] Irene Gomez: Quick security interjection - are any of the telemetry logs leaving the customer's VPC in this pilot? We need assurances about audit logs.
[01:28] Lena Ortiz: For the Dedicated pilot we kept metrics exported to a customer-controlled Prometheus in the VPC; Redwood's control plane got only aggregated health pings. We'll send the SOC2 docs and a short note about what telemetry is exported.
[01:40] Raj Patel: Perfect. Back to sizing - we had a couple of burst days last month where concurrent requests tripled for ~45 minutes. We need to plan for that without paying for that capacity 24/7.
[01:52] Devon Park: That's precisely where autoscaling + burst capacity comes in. The approach we recommend: base reserved capacity sized to cover 95th percentile sustained throughput, with a burst pool (hot spare reserved GPUs) that can be added for up to X minutes, plus policy-driven fallbacks to a cheaper model variant if capacity is constrained.
[02:12] Maya Chen: How fast can Redwood spin up the burst nodes? We can't tolerate cold start > 90 seconds for user sessions.
[02:19] Devon Park: On Dedicated with warm images and preloaded KV caches, we can get nodes served into the pool within ~40-70 seconds. Realistically you want a warm burst pool (standby) rather than cold boot. We can size warm standby as N smaller machines.
[02:33] Raj Patel: What's the cost delta for keeping a small warm standby vs. paying for overflow to hosted?
[02:38] Lena Ortiz: Cost varies by instance type; our sizing spreadsheet models both. For NovaHealth's traffic profile, a small warm standby (~1 GPU) for the peak 45-minute events is estimated at ~12% additional monthly cost versus the risk of overage on hosted or dropping to a lower-quality model. We'll attach the updated numbers.
[02:58] Sam Torres: The quality tradeoffs are important - our product team prefers consistent model outputs vs falling back to a smaller model that could change behavior.
[03:05] Devon Park: Understood. We can also employ per-route fallbacks: non-critical routes can hit a cheaper quantized variant during bursts while core assistant routes stay on the high-quality model. That's in the rollout plan.
[03:18] Maya Chen: Regarding autoscale triggers: CPU/GPU utilization vs queue length vs p95 latency - which do you recommend? We've found utilization alone to be noisy.
[03:27] Devon Park: Agreed - we recommend a hybrid policy: primary triggers on request queue length and inflight tokens, secondary guardrails on p95 latency. Utilization used only for longer-term scale decisions to avoid oscillation. Also include a cool-down window of 60-120s.
[03:40] Raj Patel: Can we set different policies for peak hours? Like more aggressive scaling in 8:30-10:30 PST.
[03:45] Devon Park: Yes, Redwood supports time-windowed autoscale policies and scheduled capacity bumps. We can pre-warm additional nodes 10 minutes before expected peaks.
[03:54] Lena Ortiz: Quick note - we pushed an updated sizing sheet earlier morning that includes a sample policy. Devon, can you walk us through the numbers?
[03:59] Devon Park: Sure. (screen share) So sheet tab A is baseline: 95th sustained RPS => 120 requests per second, average tokens per request 80, average token generation latency 18 ms per token on the chosen runtime. That maps to about 2.5 concurrent GPU slots needed, we recommended rounding to 3 for headroom. Tab B is burst calculation: observed peak multiplier 3x for 45 minutes => need additional ~6 slots; we suggest a warm standby of 2 slots plus an on-demand burst of up to 4 slots.
[04:32] Maya Chen: The metric for token generation 18 ms per token - is that measured on v4 or on quantized runtime?
[04:37] Devon Park: That's for the v4-like run with mixed precision. Quantized INT8 paths are closer to 12 ms per token but can change output slightly.
[04:46] Sam Torres: If we do the warm standby approach, what's the failure mode during extreme surge beyond 4x? Do you have graceful degradation?
[04:53] Devon Park: Yes - Redwood can enforce graceful degradation: route-level fallbacks to cached responses or smaller model variants, and queue admission control with a short retry-once policy. We'll also instrument error budgets so product can choose to fail-safe.
[05:07] Raj Patel: Let's talk about preloading KV cache. How long to preload context for the warm nodes? Does that add to spin-up time?
[05:14] Devon Park: Preloading KV cache for a customer-specific prefix (recent histories) takes about 8-12 seconds once the model is in memory. So if you're using warm standby with images that already loaded model weights, the additional overhead is small. Cold boot where weight pull is needed is the slow path.
[05:27] Irene Gomez: On the security side, what's the behavior for audit logs during scaling events? We need continuity of logs and tamper-evidence.
[05:34] Lena Ortiz: Logs are written to the customer-controlled logging endpoint; we maintain append-only operation with signed event metadata. We'll share the precise schema and retention options.
[05:44] Devon Park: Also a note - our control plane never stores raw prompt text for Dedicated if you opt out; only encrypted hashes for tracing. We documented that in the security addendum.
[05:55] Raj Patel: Circling back to cost - can you model a conservative plan where we size base for 85th percentile to save costs and rely more on burst? We are cost sensitive.
[06:04] Devon Park: Yes, we can produce two scenarios: base at 85th vs base at 95th. The 85th saves ~18% monthly but increases probability of hitting burst more frequently, which increases operational complexity. We'll include a probability-weighted cost estimate in the sheet.
[06:18] Sam Torres: For the weekly pilot, can we run a synthetic 2-hour stress run that simulates a 3x burst to validate autoscaling timings and fallbacks?
[06:25] Devon Park: Absolutely - that's actually on my action items. Plan: run the 2-hour stress on staging cluster Thursday night, capture latency, scaling events, and failure modes. We'll attach logs and Grafana snapshots.
[06:36] Maya Chen: Please also include tracing dumps for 10 slowest requests so we can see if any ops are blocking.
[06:41] Devon Park: Will do.
[06:44] Lena Ortiz: Irene, anything else on security?
[06:46] Irene Gomez: Just to confirm, we need KMS integration notes for key rotation and HSM support. If Dedicated can integrate into our cloud KMS with customer-managed keys, that's a must.
[06:56] Lena Ortiz: Redwood supports cloud KMS integrations plus HSM through our Private deployment add-on; for Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS for encryption-at-rest. We'll send the architecture note.
[07:06] Raj Patel: About failover regions - if a region is unhealthy can we fail traffic over to another region's dedicated pool? Latency will increase but availability matters.
[07:15] Devon Park: Yes, Redwood supports multi-region routing with automated fallback and model variant compatibility checks. We'll include the multi-region cost and latency estimates in the sheet.
[07:25] Sam Torres: One operational question: how do rolling updates of the model affect warm standby? Do you have a canary flow?
[07:31] Devon Park: Yes we do canary rollouts by routing a percent of traffic to the new model variant while keeping warm capacity for the old one until the canary is validated. You can also pin routes to specific versions to avoid surprises.
[07:42] Raj Patel: Good. Any open risks we should record?
[07:45] Lena Ortiz: I'll call out three: 1) Warm standby cost vs frequency of bursts (we'll quantify), 2) Quantized variant quality drift for critical routes, 3) KMS/HSM integration timeline for Dedicated - these could affect go-live.
[08:00] Maya Chen: Ok that makes sense. For the action items, Raj will push histograms, Devon runs stress, Irene confirms KMS questions.
[08:08] Lena Ortiz: Great. Quick recap and next steps: we will send the updated sizing spreadsheet with both 85th/95th scenarios and burst recommendations; Devon runs the stress test and shares logs by Friday; Redwood sends SOC2 artifacts and KMS integration note; NovaHealth to confirm which routes are critical for no-fallback behavior.
[08:30] Sam Torres: Sounds good, we'll review and pick a date for the multi-region failover test.
[08:35] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in the CRM notes and send calendar invites for the stress test.
[08:40] Raj Patel: Thanks all.
[08:42] Meeting end.
